title: Subscriptions for a physical product
metaTitle: Interval, skip, and cancel, in view
excerpt: Show the cadence, how to skip, and how to cancel beside the price. A physical subscription that is easier to start than to understand will become a dispute.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights. A repeating interior, like a shipment that still has to explain the next one.
caption: A corridor you can read as a sequence. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a physical subscription page disclose?
faqs.answer: Disclose the interval in the same words the billing system uses, the price after any intro offer, who pays shipping, what arrives, how to skip, and how to cancel. Put that block beside the price. A page that only describes the first box is selling a different product than the one you will charge for later.

faqs.question: Where should cancel live?
faqs.answer: In the account, on a phone, with a button that says cancel and a confirmation that names the last charge and the next one that will not happen. If cancel is an email, publish the address and the deadline, and read that inbox. Do not hide cancel behind a quiz or a pause that is the only control.

faqs.question: How should a gifted subscription work?
faqs.answer: Say whether the gift is a fixed number of boxes with no renewal, or a plan that will charge someone. Do not start a renewing charge on a recipient who thinks they received one box. The recipient needs the same skip and cancel facts the buyer saw, in the note that arrives with the first shipment.

markdown:
Physical product subscription UX has to explain the second shipment before the first one is easy to start. Say the interval, how to skip, and how to cancel, in the same place as the price. A subscription that is easier to begin than to understand will become a dispute, a chargeback, or a quiet grudge against the brand.

The buyer is agreeing to a series, not to a single box. If the page only describes the first box, the page is selling a different product than the one you will bill.

## The interval is part of the price

Write the cadence in days or dates a person can picture. “Every four weeks” is clearer than “monthly” if you bill every 28 days. “On the 1st” is clearer than “monthly” if that is what the warehouse runs. Use the words your billing system uses. A mismatch between the adjective and the charge date is the dispute.

Put the cadence next to the price. “$32 every four weeks, plus shipping of $6, until you cancel.” If shipping is included, say included. If the first box is discounted and the rest are not, show both numbers before the button. The first number alone is how people feel tricked on renewal, even when the terms were buried in a link.

Say what arrives. The same SKU each time, a rotating selection, or a plan they can edit. Rotating boxes need one sentence on who chooses. “We choose four coffees from the current roast list” is a product. “A surprise” is not, unless surprise is truly the product and you are willing to own the replies.

Baymard’s [cart abandonment research](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) is about single checkouts, and it still applies to the moment someone starts a plan. Extra costs sit at 40 percent of the reasons US shoppers give, and 18 percent had left because a site wanted an account. A subscription that adds a fee on the second screen, or forces an account before the cadence is visible, borrows both problems. Show the repeating total first.

## Skip and cancel are part of the offer

Say how to skip, in the product description, not only in a help doc. “Skip the next box from your account, up to three days before it ships.” If there is no skip, say there is no skip. People will assume a skip exists because other shops offer one. The assumption is how a “why did this ship” email starts.

Say how to cancel in the same block. Name the place. “Cancel in your account, under Plan, before the renew date shown there.” If cancel is an email, say the address and the deadline. “Email us two business days before the renew date.” Then staff that inbox. A cancel path you do not read is a charge they did not consent to keep.

Do not make cancel a darker pattern than subscribe. If they could start on a phone in two minutes, they should be able to stop on a phone in two minutes, without a call, a quiz, or a retained offer that hides the button. You can offer a pause after they have found cancel. You cannot offer a pause instead of cancel.

The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) puts understandable and operable next to each other. A control that looks like cancel and does not cancel fails both. Label the button with the action. “Cancel plan” ends the plan. “Pause for a month” pauses. Do not use one button for both.

Confirm the result in text. “You will not be charged again. The box that shipped on Tuesday is still on the way.” Name the last charge and the next one that will not happen. A toast that fades is not a record. Send the same facts in email.

## What the account has to show

The account is the product after the first visit. Show the next charge date, the next ship date, the amount, the address, and the status of the last box. If a payment fails, say that on this screen and in email, with a way to update the card that does not restart the plan from zero.

Let them change the address and the interval if you can operationally support the change. If a change applies only to the following box, say that. “Address updates apply to boxes that have not entered fulfillment.” A change that silently misses the box already packed will look like you ignored them.

Quantity and variant belong here if the product has them. A coffee plan that cannot change the grind is a different, stricter product. Describe the limit on the sales page so the account does not feel broken when the control is missing.

Payment updates should show the brand and the last digits, and the date the new card starts. Do not keep charging a card they removed. If a retry will run, say when, so they are not surprised by a second attempt on payday.

## The box itself

Pack a note that matches the page. What this shipment is, when the next one is scheduled, and where to skip or cancel. A card in the box is often the only reminder they will read. If it contradicts the website, the website will lose.

Tracking email should say it is the subscription box, not a one-off order. Include the renew date in that email if the next charge is soon. People forgive a cadence they can see. They dispute a cadence they have to reconstruct from bank lines.

Failed payments need a human tone and a deadline. “We could not charge the card ending 4242. Update it by Friday if you want the next box. If we do not hear from you, we will pause.” Then pause, if that is what you said. Do not keep retrying for a month in silence.

Delays in the warehouse should trigger a note before the charge if you can still stop the charge, or a note that explains the new ship date if you have already charged under a rule you disclosed. Silence plus a late box is how a subscriber cancels by charging back, which costs more than the box.

## The first order and the edge cases

Gifting a subscription is a different flow. The recipient needs to know it will renew, who pays, and how to stop it. Do not gift a renewing charge to someone who thinks they received a single box. If the gift is a fixed number of shipments, say “three boxes, no renewal.” If it renews onto their card, you are not giving a gift. You are starting a contract in their name. Do not do that.

Inventory gaps: if a SKU in the plan is unavailable, the page and the email should say what you substituted or that you skipped and did not charge. Substitution without notice is a different product in the box. Some buyers will love the replacement. The ones who write to you will not, and they are the ones who define the policy.

Price changes require notice before the new amount is charged, in the window you promised at signup or in the policy they could read. “We emailed 14 days before the new price” only counts if the email was sent and the date is true. State the new amount, the date it starts, and the cancel path in that email.

One-time add-ons should be labeled one-time. A sample tossed into the cart that becomes part of the renewal is a dark pattern even if a checkbox was involved. Show recurring and one-time as separate lines in the bag and in the account.

Down the Cove, a public ecommerce redesign, is a reminder that the shop system includes the unglamorous states: not only the campaign page, but the renewal, the skip, and the fail. If your catalog is still becoming a plan, design those screens with the product page, not after the first chargeback.

## A trial you can explain at the counter

Read the sales page aloud as if you were at a counter. Interval, price after any intro offer, who pays shipping, how to skip, how to cancel, what ships. If you cannot say it in a few sentences, the page is not ready to take a card.

Then create a test subscription with a card you control. Find the cancel control without using search. Skip a cycle if skip exists. Read every email the system sends in that week. The emails are part of the interface. A page that is clear and an email that is not will be remembered as the email.

If a sentence is only true for one plan, put it on that plan alone. A shop with two cadences needs two descriptions. A shared block of fine print will be wrong for one of them.

When the subscription is solid, the next tool some teams want is a ping in a chat app they already use, for status and simple intake, while the site keeps explaining the offer. [A Telegram bot for a business that already has a site](/blog/a-telegram-bot-for-a-business-that-already-has-a-site) covers that split.

If you are deciding whether a repeating physical product belongs in the shop you are about to build, [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) is the right place to say the interval and the cancel rule out loud before anyone draws the account screens.
